question: It took general post director Heinrich von Stephan just a few years to standardise postage rates in the newly federally constituted German Empire; what is more, in founding the Universal Postal Union in 1874, he established a cross-border tariff system for a number of sovereign states.

By contrast, the EU, in its 70 years or so of integration – and despite claiming to have a completed single market – has managed nothing of the sort. For example, sending a standard letter from Belgium to Germany via bpost currently costs EUR 3.07 – almost 2.5 times more than the EUR 1.25 Deutsche Post charges in the other direction. 1.
How does the Commission explain the persistence of such blatant tariff asymmetry for comparable cross-border correspondence within the single market?
Does it intend to bring in an initiative to harmonise or standardise cross-border postage rates; if so, when will it do so?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (4.8.2026) 1. The Postal Services Directive1 establishes the regulatory framework for postal services across the EU. The Postal Services Directive requires Member States to ensure a permanent universal service at all points of the territory at affordable prices. This concerns most notably letters and includes cross-border services. Prices shall also be cost oriented.

However, there is no legal obligation for uniform tariffs between domestic and cross border universal service letters. Asymmetric tariffs may have their reasons in different volumes, agreements and coststructures. 2. In the Single Market Strategy2 of May 2025, the Commission announced the intention to propose an EU Delivery Act to modernise the postal regulatory framework and in particular the universal service.

The aim of the EU Delivery Act would be to ensure that citizens and businesses can receive deliveries throughout the EU at affordable prices, while promoting fair competition on delivery markets and increasing consumer protection. The proposal is planned for the first quarter of 2027.
